segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The scribes and the Pharisees have seated themselves on the seat of Moses.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do and keep everything they tell you, but do not do according to their deeds, for they say and do not do.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They tie up heavy loads and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with a finger.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They do all their deeds to be seen by people: they make their phylacteries broad and their tassels long,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: they love the place of honor at dinners and the front seats in the synagogues,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the greetings in the marketplaces, and being called ‘Rabbi’ by people.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And do not call anyone on earth your father, for one is your Father, the heavenly one.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nor are you to be called instructors, because your instructor is one, the Messiah.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The greatest among you will be your servant.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of the heavens in people’s faces. For you do not go in yourselves, and those who are going in you do not allow to enter.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cross sea and dry land to make one convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as you are.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the sanctuary, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the sanctuary is bound.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blind fools! Which is greater, the gold or the sanctuary that made the gold holy?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And, ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift on it is bound.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You blind men! Which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift holy?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whoever swears by the sanctuary swears by it and by the one who dwells in it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits on it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blind guides, who strain out the gnat but swallow the camel!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of plunder and self-indulgence.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside too may become clean.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which on the outside appear beautiful but inside are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of uncleanness.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you too on the outside appear righteous to people, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and you say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in the blood of the prophets.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You, then, fill up the measure of your fathers!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Snakes, offspring of vipers! How are you to escape the judgment of Gehenna?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason, look, I am sending you prophets and wise men and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not want it!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, your house is left to you desolate.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I tell you, from now on you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

notes.note: The phrase stands for the authority to teach and apply the Law given through Moses. Stone seats of honor have been found in some ancient synagogues, and it is debated whether the expression refers to such a seat or is simply a figure of speech.

These are the small leather cases containing passages of Scripture that Jewish men strapped to the forehead and arm at prayer (tefillin), following Deuteronomy 6:8. The tassels are those the Law required on the corners of a garment (Numbers 15:38). The criticism is of enlarging both for show, not of wearing them.

The word occurs in the New Testament only in this verse. In everyday Greek of the period it commonly meant a teacher or private tutor, so 'instructors' is used here; older versions have 'masters' and some modern ones 'leaders'. It is distinct from the word translated 'teacher' in verse 8.

The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered 'Christ'. Here it has the article and functions as a title, the anointed king Israel expected, which 'Messiah' conveys to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'; the plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have heard it.

notes.phrase: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites
notes.note: The numbering passes from verse 13 to verse 15. Verse 14 in older English Bibles (a woe about devouring widows' houses and making long prayers for show) is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew and is generally thought to have been added from the similar saying in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. The edition translated here does not include it.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the image for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it 'hell', usually with a footnote; the name is kept here so that it is not merged with Hades or later imagery. 'Son of' is a Semitic idiom for one who belongs to or is destined for something.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate 'temple': one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one, which normally means the sanctuary building itself. The distinction matters in verse 35, where the altar stood in the court outside the sanctuary. Most translations use 'temple' here.

The Greek word covers both 'faith' and 'faithfulness'. Set alongside justice and mercy as a duty the Law requires, it here means the quality of being reliable and loyal, and most modern translations render it this way; older versions have 'faith'. The three terms echo prophetic summaries such as Micah 6:8.

notes.phrase: strain out the gnat but swallow the camel
notes.note: Wine was strained through cloth so as not to swallow a small insect, which the Law counted unclean. The camel was also an unclean animal and the largest one commonly seen. It is often suggested that the saying played on the similar-sounding Aramaic words for 'gnat' and 'camel'.

The murder described matches that of Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, whereas 'son of Barachiah' is the designation of the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1). How the two are related is disputed. Since Chronicles stands last in the traditional Hebrew ordering of the Scriptures, 'Abel to Zechariah' probably means from the first murder in Scripture to the last.

The 'house' may be the temple, the city of Jerusalem, or the people as a household; the temple is the most common interpretation, given what follows in the next chapter, but the others are possible. A few early manuscripts lack the word 'desolate'.

candidates.reason: English versions usually render both ναός and ἱερόν as 'temple'; whether to distinguish them consistently (sanctuary vs. temple complex) needs one decision across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
Recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts; 'scribes' suggests copyists to a modern reader, and translators vary between 'scribes', 'teachers of the law' and 'legal experts'.
Jesus' introductory 'amen' is very frequent and translators split between 'truly', 'amen' and 'I assure you'; it should be uniform across the Gospels.
The plural often covers a mixed group, and whether to render it 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' or 'siblings' needs a single policy for the Gospels and letters.
Recurs in the Gospels and Revelation; translators vary between the archaic 'woe to', 'how terrible for' and 'alas for', and a reader would be misled by variation.
